entities.summary: Hipólito José da Costa Pereira Furtado de Mendonça, born 13 August 1774, in Colonia del Sacramento, Brazil, was a Brazilian journalist and diplomat who played a pivotal role in shaping the country's press. His tenure as a journalist in Rio de Janeiro, which began in 1797, marked a turning point in Brazilian journalism, as he became a vocal advocate for press freedom and the rights of the working class. Through his writing, Hipólito da Costa sought to expose the social and economic inequalities faced by the Brazilian people, earning him the nickname 'the father of Brazilian press.' His legacy continues to inspire journalists and activists to this day, as they strive to hold those in power accountable for their actions. The establishment of the Brazilian Academy of Letters in 1936, which was largely driven by Hipólito da Costa's advocacy for press freedom, is a testament to his enduring impact on Brazilian culture. Despite facing censorship and criticism from his contemporaries, Hipólito da Costa remained committed to his craft, leaving behind a body of work that continues to be studied and admired by scholars and enthusiasts alike.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hipólito da Costa's pioneering work in shaping the Brazilian press had a lasting impact on the country's journalistic landscape and inspired a generation of Brazilian activists and journalists. His legacy continues to be felt today, as journalists and activists around the world continue to advocate for press freedom and the rights of the working class.
